newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Foreign minister seen surviving Russian reshuffle.
newsitem.headline: Foreign minister seen surviving Russian reshuffle.

text.p: Russian Foreign Minister Yevgeny Primakov is likely to be one the few survivors of a sweeping government reshuffle expected to be announced shortly.

In what seemed a clear vote of confidence in Primakov's efforts to reassert Moscow's diplomatic muscle over the past 14 months, the Kremlin has already ordered the former spymaster to Washington this weekend to prepare next week's summit between Presidents Boris Yeltsin and Bill Clinton.
Yeltsin met Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin on Thursday to discuss the government shake-up. Word of mass sackings was expected at any time. But Primakov is unlikely to be among them.

High on the agenda at the Helsinki summit on March 19 and 20 will be the search for a compromise between NATO's plans to admit former communist states in eastern Europe and Russia's fierce opposition, championed by Primakov over the past year.

Yeltsin has forecast he expects a deal. If Moscow does extract concessions for its security concerns in Europe, it will be a personal triumph for Primakov who resisted Western demands that Russia accept NATO expansion as a fait accompli.

The tough-minded Primakov, 67, replaced the soft-spoken Andrei Kozyrev in January last year amid fears in the West that he would be less amenable than Kozyrev, who was criticised at home for being too pro-Western.

The foreign minister, a former foreign intelligence service chief, kept his job during a previous reshuffle last August. Along with Interior Minister Anatoly Kulikov, he is widely seen as the most fireproof of the present cabinet team.
Primakov, an Arabic-speaker and Middle East specialist, played a key role in Moscow's efforts to prevent the Gulf War by negotiating with Iraqi leader Saddam Hussein.

Credited with considerable negotiating subtlety, Primakov has won considerable respect among Western diplomats in his latest role despite taking a tough line in the bitter row over the North Atlantic Treaty Organisation's expansion plans.

Primakov's flexibility has been seen in the way he has focused on winning a binding treaty with NATO to guarantee Russian security rather than a futile attempt to block outright the admission of former Soviet-bloc states to the Western alliance.

Primakov has also played an active role in raising Moscow's profile around the world. Though far from the level it was at during the Cold War, new initiatives in the Middle East and the Balkans, with China and elsewhere in Asia have restored a sense of self-respect to Russian diplomacy.
